frame: Tully wrote up the Mangrove Paddle Race for the island newsletter. The Moodgill's fins went gold, then grey.
text: The Mangrove Paddle Race started on a perfect morning. The channel glittered like a tray of sequins, and the crew's canoe slid along so smoothly that Tully started singing the Reef Rays club song. Mo trailed his fingers in the warm water and said this was the best race ever. Behind them, the other canoes were tiny dots, and Zed was already practising his winner's speech. By lunchtime they were in the lead. Then Zed pointed behind them. A purple cloud was creeping over the treetops like a bruise spreading across the sky. The birds stopped calling. The wind dropped, then came back cold and sudden, slapping little waves against the canoe. Tully stopped singing. 'Paddle,' she said quietly. 'Paddle now.' The first fat drops hit the water like flicked stones. They reached the finish line just as the thunder cracked. They came second, soaked to the bone, and nobody cared about the ribbon.

frame: Indi left her sketchbook open on deck. The Moodgill read her notes and went very grey.
text: Nobody had used the old jetty at Crooked Creek for thirty years. At dusk, Zed and Indi rowed out to sketch it. Indi wanted to draw the broken boathouse, and Zed wanted to prove he wasn't scared. The water was still, like a held breath. The posts leaned out of the mud like tired old men who had forgotten why they were standing there. A rusty bell hung at the end, and every so often it gave one soft clang, though there was no wind at all. Indi's pencil stopped moving. 'Did you see that?' she whispered. A light flickered in the boathouse window, pale as a moth, then went out. Zed suddenly remembered that he had left the kettle on, back on the boat, and that they should go and check it. Right now. They rowed home faster than they had ever rowed. Neither of them mentioned that the boat didn't have a kettle.

frame: Indi found this story pinned to the bakery noticeboard on Harbour Lane. The Moodgill's fins went from grey to gold.
text: Rain had been falling on Harbour Lane since breakfast, and by four o'clock the whole street looked like a photo left out in the sun to fade. Umbrellas hurried past with their heads down. Shop windows fogged over. A busker stood under the bakery awning with a battered violin case open at his feet, holding three coins and a bus ticket. Nobody looked at him. A delivery van splashed through a puddle and soaked his shoes. For a while he just tuned his strings, as if he wasn't sure anyone wanted to hear. Then he began to play. The music spilled out like warm light from an open door. A woman with a pram slowed down. A man in a soggy suit stopped checking his phone. A little boy in a yellow raincoat let go of his dad's hand and started stomping in a puddle, perfectly in time, sending up splashes that glittered under the streetlights. The baker came out, wiping her hands on her apron, and leaned in the doorway to listen. When the song ended, people clapped with wet hands and dropped coins into the case until it rattled. The rain hadn't stopped. Somehow, nobody seemed to mind anymore. The busker played until the streetlights came on.

Tully checked the sky, which was blue from edge to edge. 'Probably nothing,' she said. Mo began reeling in his line, very slowly, and suggested that the sandwiches might taste better back at the mangroves. Nobody argued.

frame: Wren wrote a note about Indi's mural for the Pelican Flat newsletter. One word is wrong.
text: When the floodwater finally drained out of Pelican Flat, it left behind a town the colour of old tea. Mud coated the footpaths, the playground and the bottom half of every shop window. Fences lay flat, as if a giant had sat on them. For two weeks, people shovelled, scrubbed and carried ruined couches out to the kerb, hardly speaking. The air smelled of wet carpet and river mud, and even the cockatoos had gone quiet. Indi was asked to paint a mural on the side of the town hall, the only wall that had stayed dry. She wasn't sure what to paint. A celebration felt wrong while half the town was still sleeping in the school gym. So she painted what she could see from the hall steps at dawn: the muddy paddocks, the broken fence posts, the crooked gum tree with a kayak still stuck in its branches. And above all of it, she painted the sun rising over the drowned paddocks like a promise someone meant to keep. On the morning the mural was finished, an old farmer stood in front of it for a long time with his hat in his hands. Then he went home and started rebuilding his fence. By the end of the week, three more fences were going up along the same road.

frame: The crew is watching Maxx Vantablack's latest live stream from Green Screen Swamp. The Moodgill has a front-row seat.
text: 'Maxx it out, Vantafam!' The MaxxCam drone swooped low over Green Screen Swamp as Maxx Vantablack stepped off his gold jet ski. Two Goldies in gold tracksuits rolled out a gold carpet across the mud, which sank almost immediately. According to his own live commentary, he strode onto the riverbank like a king arriving at his coronation, sunlight blazing off his silver hair, his brand-new gold gumboots gleaming like trophies. 'Today,' he announced, spreading his arms wide, 'I rescue the rarest Creature in the mangroves, with my bare hands.' He took one magnificent step forward. The mud took his left boot. He took another step. The mud took his right boot. For a moment he stood perfectly still in his gold socks, still smiling at the drone, while a fiddler crab strolled across his toes. Then he slowly tipped backwards into the swamp, with a sound like a giant slurping the last of a milkshake. The drone kept filming. Somewhere, millions of Vantafam watched the bubbles rise. Up in the mangroves, the Moodgill made a noise that sounded suspiciously like laughing. 'That's Maxx-imum content!' gurgled Maxx, from somewhere under the mud. 'Stay gold!' The Goldies looked at each other, then went to find a very long stick.

passage: Gus called it Experiment 47, and he had promised the crew it was completely safe. He had said the same about Experiments 1 to 46, and most of those had ended with the fire extinguisher. [The lab was as tidy as a dentist's waiting room, with every jar labelled and every spoon in a row.] He tipped a spoonful of green powder into a bucket of swamp water and stirred. At first, nothing happened. Then the mixture began to bubble, and a smell like a thousand forgotten lunchboxes rolled across the room. [Mo gagged like a cat with a hairball.] The slime rose over the rim of the bucket. [It crept across the bench like something hungry that had just woken up, feeling its way towards Gus's sandwich.] Gus took a careful step back. 'Interesting,' he said, in a voice that was trying hard to sound calm. [Outside the porthole, the sunset glowed like a bowl of warm peaches.] The slime reached the sandwich and swallowed it with a soft, satisfied gloop. Then it turned, very slowly, towards the crew. 'That's not gross,' whispered Gus. 'That's science.' Nobody stayed to argue. The Moodgill stayed in the mud until dinner. Later, Gus wrote one word in his notebook: SUCCESS.
